title: Knowing and doing
hookLine: Arjuna begs Krishna to just pick one, and the Isha refuses too
tomorrow: The face of truth, covered in gold

lines: THE WISE SEE THEM AS ONE.
cards: Remember Arjuna in the chariot. Krishna has praised knowledge, the quiet wisdom that sees the self. Then he's praised action, doing your duty.

And at the start of chapter three, Arjuna says what every confused student says: if knowledge is better than action, why push me into this terrible work? You're mixing me up. Tell me the one thing, for certain.
In chapter five he tries again: you praise giving up action, then you praise doing it. Which is better? Just pick one.
Krishna's answer: only children talk as if the two are different. The wise see them as one.

teach.b: The Isha makes the same refusal, in its own strange way. Verse nine: into blind darkness go those who follow avidya, not-knowing.
Into a greater darkness, as it were, go those who delight in vidya, knowing, alone. Knowledge on its own gets the worse darkness. What do the words mean here?
The text doesn't define them, and scholars still argue. Shankara took vidya as meditation, inner knowing, and avidya as ritual and work in the world.

However you read them, verse eleven says what to do: the one who knows both together crosses death by the one and reaches the deathless by the other. Verses twelve to fourteen run the same pattern with another pair.
This is a big Hindu teaching: wisdom and practice belong together. Jnana, knowing, and karma, doing, aren't rival teams. You can see it in an ordinary Hindu evening.
Someone lights the lamp and waves it for aarti: the hands, doing.

teach.h: THE LAMP, AND WHAT IT MEANS.
teach.b: And the same person may know what many say the flame means: light offered back to the source of light.
Without the knowing, a ritual can go hollow. Without the doing, knowing floats off and gets proud, which may be why the Isha gives knowledge alone the darker place. Arjuna wanted one answer.
Both texts give him two, held in one hand.

how: Hindu teachers of different schools read Isha verses 9–14 differently, but the verses are commonly taught as a call to hold inner knowledge and outer action together.

games.q: the paired opposites — tap the pairs.

s: the Isha says knowledge alone leads to a greater darkness
verse nine: into greater darkness, as it were, go those who delight in vidya alone.
the text clearly defines vidya and avidya
it doesn't; commentators and scholars still argue about what they mean here.
the Isha asks you to choose knowing over doing
it says know both together: cross death by one, reach the deathless by the other.

games.q: arjuna asks krishna: knowledge or action, which is better? what do the Gita and the Isha answer?
o: both together; either alone goes dark.
games.why: Gita 5.4: only children say they're different. Isha 11: know both together.

practice: If you have a lamp, a candle or a diya, light it, or just picture one: that's the doing. Then say, aloud or inside, one line you've learned this week, maybe isha vasyam idam sarvam: that's the knowing.
Hold the two together for a few breaths, the flame and its meaning. If you don't pray, let the light be a small act of care, and the line a thought to carry with it.

wordCard.voice: Vidya, knowledge, from vid, to know. The one who knows vidya and avidya together crosses death and gains the deathless; follow only one and it goes dark.

orig.note: Sanskrit: vidya, knowledge; from vid, to know, the same root as Veda. Avidya is not-knowing.

carryVoice: Your line: knowing and doing, held together. Either one alone goes dark. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.1–2 and 5.1–5 (Arjuna asks which is better; the wise see knowledge and action as one)
